room: It was a voluptuous scene, that masquerade. But first let me speak of the rooms in which it was held. There were seven imperial suites.

The rooms were so irregular that the view reached only a little at a time: there was a sharp turn every twenty or thirty meters, and at each turn a new effect. To the right and left, in the middle of each wall, a tall and narrow Gothic window looked out upon a closed corridor that followed the winding of the room. These windows were stained glass whose color varied according to the prevailing tone of the decorations of the chamber in which they opened.

No light came from lamps or candles within the suite of chambers. But in the corridors that followed the suite, opposite each window, there stood a heavy tripod with a brazier of fire, which threw its rays through the colored glass and illuminated the room with shimmering light. And thus an infinity of exuberant fantastic appearances was produced.

One had to hear him, see him, and touch him to be sure that he was not. He had largely directed the decoration of the seven rooms for this grand fête and also chosen the costumes of the masked guests. They were grotesque.

There was much that was lovely, much that was licentious, much that was bizarre, terrible things, and not a little that could be considered disgusting. From one end to the other of the seven rooms there was, indeed, a multitude of dreams. And these—those dreams—twisted themselves, drawing tone from the rooms and making the wild music of the orchestra seem the echo of their steps.

Those whose feet trod the velvet carpet would hear the muffled sound of the clock, and hear it more solemnly and emphatically than the guests in the other chambers. But the other rooms were densely crowded, and in them throbbed the heart of life. And the feast continued to whirl until finally the stroke of midnight began to sound on the clock.

Seize him and unmask him—so that we may know whom we are to hang at sunrise!” It was in the eastern, or blue, room that Prince Prospero stood while pronouncing these words. They echoed through the seven rooms, loud and clear—for the prince was a bold and robust man, and the music was stifled by a motion of his hand.

The stranger, who was near at hand, and with deliberate and imposing step, approached the speaker more closely. But no one was found who stretched out a hand to seize him; so that, unimpeded, he passed within a meter of the prince’s person; and, while the vast assembly, as if by a single impulse, recoiled from the center of the rooms to the walls, he continued unbroken with the same solemn and measured step, through the blue chamber to the purple—through the purple to the green—through the green to the orange—through that again to the white—and even from there to the violet without anyone to stop him. It was then, however, that Prospero himself, maddened with rage and ashamed of his momentary cowardice, rushed hurriedly through the six chambers, while no one followed him.
blood: No pestilence had ever been so fatal or so hideous. The Red Death bore the blood as its avatar and its seal—the redness and the horror of blood. Those infected suffered sharp pains, sudden dizziness, and then profuse bleeding from their pores, followed by decomposition.

The seventh room was wrapped in black velvet hangings suspended from the entire ceiling and walls, falling in heavy folds over a carpet of the same material and color. And, in this chamber alone, the color of the windows did not correspond to the decorations: the panes were scarlet—deep blood-red. In none of the seven rooms was there a lamp or chandelier hanging from the ornamented gold ceiling.

And thus an infinity of exuberant fantastic appearances was produced. But, in the last room, the black one, the effect of the firelight flowing over the dark draperies through the blood-stained panes was horrible to the extreme, inspiring terror in the faces of those who entered, so that few were bold enough to go in. In this same room, against the western wall, stood a gigantic ebony clock.

And now once again the music began, and the dreams lived, and twisted themselves more and more gaily than ever, taking color from the many tinted windows through which the rays of the tripods flowed. But to the room farthest west of the seven, none of the masked guests ventured; because, as the night advanced, the light filtered by the blood-colored panes grew redder, and the black draperies made the darkness more fearful. Those whose feet trod the velvet carpet would hear the muffled sound of the clock, and hear it more solemnly and emphatically than the guests in the other chambers.

But the masked figure had gone so far as to disguise himself as the Red Death. His garments were drenched in blood—and his broad brow, with all the features of the face, was stained with the red marks. When Prince Prospero’s eyes fell upon this spectral image (which, with a slow and solemn movement, in order to sustain his role, was walking to and fro among the waltzes), he convulsed at first with a strong shudder of terror or aversion; but a moment later his forehead flushed with rage.

It came as a thief in the night. And one by one it laid low the revellers in the blood-stained halls, each dying in the desperate posture of his fall. And the life of the ebony clock ended with that of the last reveller.
